sections.text:
A **statistical question** expects answers that **vary**.

"How many pets do kids in my class have?" got these answers from 10 kids: 0, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4, 5. Lots of different answers!
"How many pets does Andrew have?" is **not** statistical. It has just one answer: 2.
**Tip:** to make a question statistical, ask *many people* or measure *many times*.

learn.keyIdea: A statistical question collects many answers that vary.

examples.title: Spot the statistical ones
examples.prompt: How many of these are statistical questions? (A) How old is Andrew? (B) How old are the students at Andrew's school? (C) How many minutes do sixth graders spend on homework? (D) What time does school start?

steps.do: Check A: one person, one age.
steps.why: A question about one person cannot vary.

steps.do: Check B and C: many people, many answers.
steps.why: Different people give different answers.

steps.do: Check D: school starts at one time.
steps.why: There is only one start time.

steps.do: Count the statistical ones: B and C make 2.
steps.why: Only B and C expect variability.

examples.check: B and C ask groups, and A and D ask about one thing. ✅
examples.mistake: "How old is Andrew?" sounds like math, but one answer means it is not statistical.

examples.title: How many data values?
examples.prompt: Andrew asks 25 classmates, "How many pets do you have?" How many data values will he collect?

steps.why: One person gives one data value.
Count every answer, even repeats.

examples.check: Even if 5 classmates say 0 pets, each one counts. ✅
examples.mistake: Don't count only the different answers; repeats are still data values.

examples.title: Reading the answers
examples.prompt: Ten classmates said how many pets they have: 0, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4, 5. How many different answers are there?

steps.why: We want the different answers only.
Each value is one different answer.

examples.check: The dot plot has stacks at 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5. ✅
examples.mistake: Don't count all 10 answers; the question asks for different answers.

sections.text:
Every data set has a **center**, a **spread**, and a **shape**.

This dot plot is **symmetric**: 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 4, 4, 5. Its center is 3 and its range is 5 − 1 = 4.

When the dots pile up on one side and a **tail** stretches out, the data is **skewed**.

Here: 1, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 6. The tail goes right, so it is **skewed right**.
Look for **peaks** (tall stacks), **clusters** (bunches), and **gaps** (empty spots). In the plot above, there is a gap at 4 and 5.

learn.keyIdea: Describe data with its center, its spread, and its overall shape.

examples.title: Range from a dot plot
examples.prompt: A dot plot of quiz scores shows 1: 1 dot; 2: 2 dots; 3: 5 dots; 4: 3 dots; 6: 1 dot. What is the range?

steps.why: The range uses the smallest value.
The range uses the biggest value.
Range shows how spread out the data is.

examples.mistake: Don't subtract the counts of dots; use the values on the number line.

examples.title: Find the peak
examples.prompt: A dot plot of hot lunches bought shows 1: 6 dots; 2: 4 dots; 3: 2 dots; 6: 1 dot. At which value is the peak?

steps.why: The peak is where the most data piles up.

steps.do: The tallest stack sits at the value 1.
steps.why: The peak is a value, not a count of dots.

examples.mistake: The answer is the value (1), not how many dots are in the stack (6).

examples.title: Median from a dot plot
examples.prompt: A dot plot of minutes of recess shows 4: 1 dot; 5: 7 dots; 6: 3 dots; 8: 1 dot. What is the median?

steps.why: We need to know where the middle is.

steps.do: With 12 dots the middle is between the 6th and 7th dots.
steps.why: An even count has two middle values.

steps.do: Count from the left: the 6th and 7th dots are both 5, so the median is 5.
steps.why: Both middles are in the stack at 5.

examples.check: 6 dots are at 5 or below on the low side and 6 at 5 or above on the high side. ✅
examples.mistake: Don't pick the middle of the number line; count the dots.

guided.prompt: A dot plot shows 10: 1 dot; 11: 3 dots; 12: 6 dots; 13: 2 dots; 15: 2 dots. What is the range?

steps.why: Range starts at the lowest data value.
Range ends at the highest data value.
Range is max minus min.

guided.prompt: A dot plot shows 10: 1 dot; 11: 3 dots; 12: 6 dots; 13: 2 dots; 15: 2 dots. At which value is the peak?

steps.do: How many dots are in the tallest stack?
steps.why: The tallest stack is the peak.

steps.do: At which value is that stack?
steps.why: The peak is named by its value.

guided.prompt: Dots pile up on the left (1: 6 dots; 2: 4 dots) and thin out to the right (3: 2 dots; 4: 1 dot; 5: 1 dot). What is the shape?

steps.do: Which side has the long thin tail?
steps.why: Skew is named for the side with the tail.

choices: left
right
neither

steps.hint: Where are there only 1 or 2 dots?
steps.worked: The tail is on the right.

steps.why: A right tail means skewed right.

choices: symmetric
skewed right
skewed left
uniform

guided.prompt: A dot plot shows 2: 1 dot; 3: 2 dots; 4: 2 dots; 6: 2 dots. What is the median?

steps.why: We need the count to find the middle.

steps.do: Which dot is in the middle?
steps.why: With 7 dots, the 4th dot has 3 on each side.
The median is the value of the middle dot.

topics.title: Center Stage: Mean, Median, Mode & Range

sections.text:
A **measure of center** sums up data with one number.

The **mean** is the fair share: for 2, 4, 9 the total is 15 and 15 ÷ 3 = **5**.
The **median** is the middle value in order. For 3, 5, 7, 9 the middles are 5 and 7, so the median is **6**.
The **mode** is the most common value, and the **range** (max − min) measures spread. For 4, 6, 6, 10 the mode is 6 and the range is 10 − 4 = 6.

learn.keyIdea: Center (mean, median, mode) tells what's typical, and variation (range) tells how spread out the data is.

examples.title: Fair share mean

steps.why: The mean shares the total equally.
There are 3 values to share among.

examples.mistake: Divide by how many values there are (3), not by the biggest value.

examples.title: Median of an even list

steps.why: The median is the middle of an ordered list.

steps.do: The two middle values are 5 and 7.
steps.why: An even count has two middles.
The median sits halfway between the two middles.

examples.check: Two values are below 6 and two are above. ✅
examples.mistake: Don't take the middle of the unordered list (3 and 9); order first.

examples.title: Range

steps.do: Find the max (10) and the min (4).
steps.why: Range compares the two ends.
The difference shows the spread.

examples.check: From 4 to 10 is 6 steps on a number line. ✅
examples.mistake: The mode is also 6 here, but range and mode mean different things.

guided.prompt: Find the mean of 4, 6, 8, and 10.

steps.why: The mean starts with the total.

steps.do: Divide by the number of values.
steps.why: There are 4 values to share the total.

guided.prompt: Find the median of 15, 11, 20, 14, 13, 17.

steps.do: Order the values. Which value is 3rd?
steps.why: An ordered list shows the middle.
With 6 values, the 3rd and 4th are the middles.
The median is halfway between them.

guided.prompt: Find the range of 45, 52, 38, 61, 49.

steps.why: Range uses the biggest value.
Range uses the smallest value.
The gap shows how spread out the data is.

guided.prompt: Andrew's scores are 80, 90, and 85. What must his next score be so his mean is 86?

steps.do: What total do 4 scores need for a mean of 86?
steps.why: Mean × count = total.

steps.do: What is the total so far?
steps.why: Add his 3 scores.

steps.do: What score makes up the difference?
steps.why: The next score fills the gap.

topics.title: Picture Power: Dot Plots, Histograms & Box Plots

sections.text:
A **dot plot** puts one dot above the number line for each value.

Scores 2, 3, 3, 3, 4, 5 make a tall stack at 3.
A **histogram** groups values into intervals and draws a bar for each one. For the ages 3, 8, 12, 14, 19, the bar for 10 to 19 is 3 tall.
A **box plot** shows five numbers: min, Q₁, median, Q₃, max. For 1, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9, 11 they are 1, 3, 6, 9, 11. Each of the four sections holds about 25% of the data.

learn.keyIdea: Dot plots show every value, histograms count values in intervals, and box plots show the five-number summary.

examples.title: Histogram bar
examples.prompt: Ages at a party: 3, 8, 12, 14, 19. A histogram has a bar for ages 10 to 19. How tall is that bar?

steps.why: A histogram bar counts values in its interval.
The bar's height is how many values landed there.

examples.check: 3 and 8 belong in the 0 to 9 bar, so 2 + 3 = 5 ages total. ✅
examples.mistake: Don't make the bar's height the biggest age (19); bars show counts.

examples.title: Five-number summary
examples.prompt: Find Q₃ for the box plot of 1, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9, 11.

steps.do: The median of 7 values is the 4th: 6.
steps.why: The median splits the data in half.

steps.do: The upper half (leave out the median) is 8, 9, 11.
steps.why: Q₃ is the middle of the upper half.
steps.rule: Upper half = values above the median

steps.why: That value marks the right edge of the box.

examples.check: About a quarter of the data (11) is above 9. ✅
examples.mistake: Don't include the median itself in the upper half when the count is odd.

examples.title: IQR from a box plot
examples.prompt: A box plot has min 1, Q₁ = 3, median 6, Q₃ = 9, and max 11. What is the IQR?

steps.why: The IQR is the width of the box.

examples.check: The middle half of the data spans 6 units. ✅
examples.mistake: Don't use max − min; that is the range, not the IQR.

guided.prompt: Ages at a party: 41, 45, 52, 58, 60, 63, 67, 71, 74. How many ages are in the 60 to 69 bar of a histogram?

steps.do: Which is the smallest age in that interval?
steps.why: The bar starts at 60.
The bar's height is this count.

guided.prompt: A box plot shows min 10, Q₁ 14, median 18, Q₃ 25, max 30. What is the IQR?

steps.do: Which two numbers make the box?
steps.why: The box runs from Q₁ to Q₃.

choices: 10 and 30
14 and 25
14 and 18
18 and 25

steps.hint: The box edges are the quartiles.

steps.why: The IQR is the width of the box.

guided.prompt: A box plot has min 50, Q₁ = 55, median = 62, Q₃ = 70, and max 88. About what percent of the data is above 70?

steps.do: How many equal parts does a box plot split data into?
steps.why: Each section holds the same share.
steps.hint: Min to Q₁, Q₁ to median, median to Q₃, Q₃ to max.

steps.do: What percent is in the part above Q₃?
steps.why: Each of 4 equal parts is 100 ÷ 4 percent.

guided.prompt: For the data 2, 4, 4, 6, 9, 10, 13, 15, 17, what is the IQR?

steps.why: The median splits the data in half.
Q₁ is the middle of the lower half.
Q₃ is the middle of the upper half.
IQR is the spread of the middle half.

sections.text:
The **MAD** (mean absolute deviation) is the average distance from the mean.

For 2, 4, 6, 8 the mean is 5, the distances are 3, 1, 1, 3, and the MAD is 8 ÷ 4 = **2**.
An **outlier** is far from the rest. In 3, 4, 4, 5, 50 the mean is 13.2 but the median is 4. Use **median and IQR** when there are outliers or skew.
For **symmetric** data with no outliers, the **mean and MAD** work great. Always say how many values you have and what was measured.

learn.keyIdea: Outliers or skew? Use median and IQR. Symmetric? Use mean and MAD.

examples.title: Mean absolute deviation

steps.why: MAD measures distance from the mean.
Distances are never negative.
MAD is the typical distance from the mean.

examples.check: On average, each value is 2 away from 5. ✅
examples.mistake: Don't stop at adding the distances (8); divide by the count too.

examples.title: Outlier alert
examples.prompt: For 3, 4, 4, 5, 50, which is more typical, the mean or the median? Find the median.

steps.why: The mean uses every value, even outliers.

steps.do: Find the median: the 3rd value is 4.
steps.why: The median only cares about the middle.

steps.do: Pick the median, 4, as the typical value.
steps.why: The outlier 50 pulls the mean far from most data.

examples.check: Four of the five values are near 4, not 13.2. ✅
examples.mistake: Don't trust the mean when there's an outlier; it gets pulled toward it.

examples.title: IQR of a data set

steps.why: Q₁ is the median of the lower half.
Q₃ is the median of the upper half.
The IQR is the spread of the middle half.

examples.check: The middle half, from 2 to 7, spans 5. ✅
examples.mistake: Don't subtract the min from the max; that's the range (8).

guided.prompt: Five friends earned $5, $6, $5, $7, and $90. Which measure of center best describes a typical amount?

steps.why: An outlier is far from the rest of the data.

choices: Yes
No

steps.do: Choose the best measure of center.
steps.why: The median is not pulled by outliers.

choices: mean
median
range
MAD

guided.prompt: Find the MAD of 3, 5, 7, 9, 11.

steps.why: MAD measures distance from the mean.
Distances are 4, 2, 0, 2, 4.
MAD is the average distance.

guided.prompt: Test scores were 78, 80, 82, 81, 79 with no outliers. Which pair of measures summarizes the data best?

steps.do: Is the data roughly symmetric with no outliers?
steps.why: Symmetric data lets the mean be typical.

choices: Yes
No

steps.why: With no outliers, mean and MAD use every value well.

choices: median and range
mode and IQR
mean and MAD
max and min

steps.hint: Center and spread that go together.

guided.prompt: Find the MAD of 2, 5, 6, 9, 13.

steps.why: MAD measures distance from the mean.
Distances are 5, 2, 1, 2, 6.
MAD is the average distance.
